question.text: Ms. Arushi Bhatia holds 5% in 'Priya Foods Pvt Ltd'. 'Lotus Ventures' Cat II AIF holds ROFR over her shares. Arushi receives a market offer of INR 500/share from a third party. Lotus Ventures is willing to pay INR 450. Under ROFR:

answer.text: Arushi must sell to Lotus at INR 450 since Lotus holds ROFR
Lotus has a veto and can block the entire sale
Arushi can freely sell to the third party at INR 500 without any offer to Lotus
Arushi must offer the shares to Lotus at INR 500 (the best market quote); if Lotus matches, it buys; if Lotus refuses, Arushi sells to the third party at INR 500

explanation.text: The Logic: Per the AIF Managers workbook on exit rights (p. 296), under ROFR the selling shareholder must approach the ROFR-holder with the best quote obtained from market participants. The ROFR-holder then chooses to buy by matching that best quote, or refuses. Arushi's best market quote is INR 500, so she must offer the shares to Lotus at INR 500. Lotus cannot dictate a lower price; it must either match INR 500 or refuse and allow Arushi to sell to the third party at INR 500. The Trap: Option A treats ROFR like a call option at a Lotus-chosen price, which is not how p. 296 describes the right. Option B describes a veto right, not a ROFR; a veto would let Lotus block the sale altogether, which is a different exit-right construct. Option C ignores the ROFR entirely. Note: The ROFR right on p. 296 is anchored on the selling shareholder presenting the best market quote and the ROFR-holder either matching it or refusing.
